classification.difficultyReason: Identify the π/6 or π/3 reference angle, apply the quadrant signs to sine and cosine, and obtain tangent from their ratio. These are direct applications of taught exact-ratio methods; the repeated columns add no new reasoning demand.

answer.worked:
$\frac{\pi}{6}$ is in quadrant I. The exact $30^\circ$ ratios give $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac12$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{\pi}{6}&=\frac{\sin\frac{\pi}{6}}{\cos\frac{\pi}{6}}\\\tan\frac{\pi}{6}&=\frac{\frac12}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}\\\tan\frac{\pi}{6}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\end{aligned}$

$\frac{\pi}{3}$ is in quadrant I. The exact $60^\circ$ ratios give $\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac12$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{\pi}{3}&=\frac{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{\cos\frac{\pi}{3}}\\\tan\frac{\pi}{3}&=\frac{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac12}\\\tan\frac{\pi}{3}&=\sqrt3\end{aligned}$

$\frac{2\pi}{3}=\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}$ lies in quadrant II, with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$. Sine is positive and cosine is negative, so $\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac12$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{2\pi}{3}&=\frac{\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}}{\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}}\\\tan\frac{2\pi}{3}&=\frac{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{-\frac12}\\\tan\frac{2\pi}{3}&=-\sqrt3\end{aligned}$

$\frac{5\pi}{6}=\pi-\frac{\pi}{6}$ lies in quadrant II, with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$. Sine is positive and cosine is negative, so $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac12$ and $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{5\pi}{6}&=\frac{\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}}{\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}}\\\tan\frac{5\pi}{6}&=\frac{\frac12}{-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}\\\tan\frac{5\pi}{6}&=-\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\end{aligned}$

$\frac{7\pi}{6}=\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}$ lies in quadrant III, with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$. Sine and cosine are negative, so $\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}=-\frac12$ and $\cos\frac{7\pi}{6}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{7\pi}{6}&=\frac{\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}}{\cos\frac{7\pi}{6}}\\\tan\frac{7\pi}{6}&=\frac{-\frac12}{-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}\\\tan\frac{7\pi}{6}&=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\end{aligned}$

$\frac{4\pi}{3}=\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}$ lies in quadrant III, with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$. Sine and cosine are negative, so $\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}=-\frac12$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{4\pi}{3}&=\frac{\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}}{\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}}\\\tan\frac{4\pi}{3}&=\frac{-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{-\frac12}\\\tan\frac{4\pi}{3}&=\sqrt3\end{aligned}$

$\frac{5\pi}{3}=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}$ lies in quadrant IV, with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$. Sine is negative and cosine is positive.

$\sin\frac{5\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\frac{5\pi}{3}=\frac12$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}&=\frac{\sin\frac{5\pi}{3}}{\cos\frac{5\pi}{3}}\\\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}&=\frac{-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac12}\\\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}&=-\sqrt3\end{aligned}$

$\frac{11\pi}{6}=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{6}$ lies in quadrant IV, with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$. Sine is negative and cosine is positive.

$\sin\frac{11\pi}{6}=-\frac12$ and $\cos\frac{11\pi}{6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{11\pi}{6}&=\frac{\sin\frac{11\pi}{6}}{\cos\frac{11\pi}{6}}\\\tan\frac{11\pi}{6}&=\frac{-\frac12}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}\\\tan\frac{11\pi}{6}&=-\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\end{aligned}$

classification.difficultyReason: Apply exact π/4 ratios and quadrant signs, read quadrantal values from unit-circle coordinates, and identify undefined tangent when cosine is zero. These are direct taught applications; repeated table entries add no new reasoning demand.

answer.worked:
At $\theta=0$, the unit-circle point is $(1,0)$, so $\cos0=1$ and $\sin0=0$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan0&=\frac{\sin0}{\cos0}\\\tan0&=\frac01\\\tan0&=0\end{aligned}$

$\frac{\pi}{4}$ is in quadrant I. The exact $45^\circ$ ratios give $\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{\pi}{4}&=\frac{\sin\frac{\pi}{4}}{\cos\frac{\pi}{4}}\\\tan\frac{\pi}{4}&=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\\\tan\frac{\pi}{4}&=1\end{aligned}$

At $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$, the unit-circle point is $(0,1)$, so $\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1$ and $\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0$.

$\tan\frac{\pi}{2}$ is undefined because $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ would require division by zero.

$\frac{3\pi}{4}=\pi-\frac{\pi}{4}$ lies in quadrant II. With reference angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$, sine is positive and cosine is negative: $\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{3\pi}{4}&=\frac{\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}}{\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}}\\\tan\frac{3\pi}{4}&=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}{-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\\\tan\frac{3\pi}{4}&=-1\end{aligned}$

At $\theta=\pi$, the unit-circle point is $(-1,0)$, so $\sin\pi=0$ and $\cos\pi=-1$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\pi&=\frac{\sin\pi}{\cos\pi}\\\tan\pi&=\frac{0}{-1}\\\tan\pi&=0\end{aligned}$

$\frac{5\pi}{4}=\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}$ lies in quadrant III. With reference angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$, sine and cosine are negative: $\sin\frac{5\pi}{4}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\cos\frac{5\pi}{4}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{5\pi}{4}&=\frac{\sin\frac{5\pi}{4}}{\cos\frac{5\pi}{4}}\\\tan\frac{5\pi}{4}&=\frac{-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}{-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\\\tan\frac{5\pi}{4}&=1\end{aligned}$

At $\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}$, the unit-circle point is $(0,-1)$, so $\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=-1$ and $\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}=0$.

$\tan\frac{3\pi}{2}$ is undefined because $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ would require division by zero.

$\frac{7\pi}{4}=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{4}$ lies in quadrant IV. With reference angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$, sine is negative and cosine is positive: $\sin\frac{7\pi}{4}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\cos\frac{7\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan\frac{7\pi}{4}&=\frac{\sin\frac{7\pi}{4}}{\cos\frac{7\pi}{4}}\\\tan\frac{7\pi}{4}&=\frac{-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}\\\tan\frac{7\pi}{4}&=-1\end{aligned}$

At $\theta=2\pi$, the unit-circle point is $(1,0)$, so $\sin2\pi=0$ and $\cos2\pi=1$.

$\begin{aligned}\tan2\pi&=\frac{\sin2\pi}{\cos2\pi}\\\tan2\pi&=\frac01\\\tan2\pi&=0\end{aligned}$

answer.worked:
Reflection in the $y$-axis preserves the sine value.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(\pi-\theta)&=\sin\theta\end{align*}$$

Reflection in the $y$-axis reverses the cosine sign.
$$\begin{align*}\cos(\pi-\theta)&=-\cos\theta\end{align*}$$

Reflection in the $y$-axis preserves sine and reverses cosine.
$$\begin{align*}\tan(\pi-\theta)&=\frac{\sin\theta}{-\cos\theta}\\\tan(\pi-\theta)&=-\tan\theta\end{align*}$$

A half-turn reverses the sine sign.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(\pi+\theta)&=-\sin\theta\end{align*}$$

A half-turn reverses the cosine sign.
$$\begin{align*}\cos(\pi+\theta)&=-\cos\theta\end{align*}$$

A half-turn reverses both sine and cosine, preserving their quotient.
$$\begin{align*}\tan(\pi+\theta)&=\frac{-\sin\theta}{-\cos\theta}\\\tan(\pi+\theta)&=\tan\theta\end{align*}$$

Reflection in the $x$-axis reverses the sine sign.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(2\pi-\theta)&=-\sin\theta\end{align*}$$

Reflection in the $x$-axis preserves the cosine value.
$$\begin{align*}\cos(2\pi-\theta)&=\cos\theta\end{align*}$$

Reflection in the $x$-axis reverses sine and preserves cosine.
$$\begin{align*}\tan(2\pi-\theta)&=\frac{-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\\\tan(2\pi-\theta)&=-\tan\theta\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Suppose $\sin\theta=0.7$. Use the diagram from Question 10 to help you find the value of

answer.worked:
Reflection in the $y$-axis preserves sine.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(\pi-\theta)&=\sin\theta\\\sin(\pi-\theta)&=0.7\end{align*}$$

Reflection in the $x$-axis reverses the sine sign.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(2\pi-\theta)&=-\sin\theta\\\sin(2\pi-\theta)&=-0.7\end{align*}$$

A half-turn reverses the sine sign.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(\pi+\theta)&=-\sin\theta\\\sin(\pi+\theta)&=-0.7\end{align*}$$

The angles $-\theta$ and $\theta$ are reflections in the $x$-axis, so their sine values have opposite signs.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(-\theta)&=-\sin\theta\\\sin(-\theta)&=-0.7\end{align*}$$

Adding a full turn preserves the sine value.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(2\pi+\theta)&=\sin\theta\\\sin(2\pi+\theta)&=0.7\end{align*}$$

Removing two full turns gives $-\theta$; reflection in the $x$-axis reverses sine.
$$\begin{align*}\sin(4\pi-\theta)&=\sin(-\theta)\\\sin(4\pi-\theta)&=-\sin\theta\\\sin(4\pi-\theta)&=-0.7\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
[Small angle approximation]

The diagram below shows $\theta$ radians on the unit circle, where $\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

spec.description: First-quadrant unit-circle arc with P on the circle, Q on the extension of OP directly above Q′=(1,0), and perpendicular feet P′ and Q′. The highlighted arc runs from P to Q′. The illustrative 50-degree construction parameter is unprinted and does not constrain the variable angle.

spec.answerVisibility: All labels, guides and coloured distinctions are permanent question givens; no derived lengths or answers are shown.

answer.worked:
In right triangle $OPP'$, $OP=1$.
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta&=\frac{PP'}{OP}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{PP'}{1}\\PP'&=\sin\theta\end{align*}$$

In right triangle $OQQ'$, $OQ'=1$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{QQ'}{OQ'}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{QQ'}{1}\\QQ'&=\tan\theta\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Briefly explain why the arc length $\widehat{PQ'}=\theta$.

answer.short: On the unit circle, arc length $=r\theta=1\times\theta=\theta$.
answer.worked:
The arc subtends $\theta$ radians at the centre. By the definition of radian measure,
$$\begin{align*}\text{arc length }\widehat{PQ'}&=r\theta\\\text{arc length }\widehat{PQ'}&=1\times\theta=\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: What can we say about the lengths $PP'$, $QQ'$ and the arc $\widehat{PQ'}$ in comparison to each other, if $\theta$ is a small angle?

answer.worked:
For a small positive angle, the two perpendicular lengths and the intervening arc length are approximately equal:
$$PP'\approx QQ'\approx\text{arc length }\widehat{PQ'}.$$
Thus $\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta\approx\theta$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Hence find the approximate value of $\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}$ and $\frac{\tan\theta}{\theta}$ if $\theta\approx0$.

answer.worked:
For small positive $\theta$ measured in radians, $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ and $\tan\theta\approx\theta$. Since $\theta\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}&\approx\frac{\theta}{\theta}=1\\\frac{\tan\theta}{\theta}&\approx\frac{\theta}{\theta}=1.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Calculate $\angle ABC$ in radians, correct to three decimal places.

answer.worked:
In right-angled $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\cos\angle ABC&=\frac{BC}{BA}\\\cos\angle ABC&=\frac{5}{13}\\\angle ABC&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)\\\angle ABC&\approx1.176\text{ radians}.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Calculate the length of the minor arc $CD$, correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
The right triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$ are congruent: they share hypotenuse $AB$ and have equal radii $BC$ and $BD$. Hence $\angle CBD=2\angle ABC$.

$$\begin{align*}\theta_{\text{minor}}&=2\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)\\l_{\text{minor}}&=r\theta_{\text{minor}}\\l_{\text{minor}}&=5\left[2\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)\right]\\l_{\text{minor}}&\approx11.76\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:

$$\begin{align*}l_{\text{major}}&=2\pi r-l_{\text{minor}}\\l_{\text{major}}&=10\pi-10\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)\\l_{\text{major}}&\approx19.66\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the area of $\triangle OPQ'=\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta$.

answer.worked:
The unit-circle radii give $OP=OQ'=1$, and the included angle is $\theta$.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\triangle OPQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}\,OP\cdot OQ'\sin\theta\\A_{\triangle OPQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}(1)(1)\sin\theta\\A_{\triangle OPQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the area of $\triangle OQQ'=\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$.

answer.worked:
In the right triangle $OQQ'$, the adjacent side is $OQ'=1$.

$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{Q'Q}{OQ'}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{Q'Q}{1}\\Q'Q&=\tan\theta.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}A_{\triangle OQQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}\,OQ'\cdot Q'Q\\A_{\triangle OQQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}(1)\tan\theta\\A_{\triangle OQQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
By finding the area of sector $OPQ'$ and comparing it to the areas from parts (a) and (b), show that for $\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$,

$$\sin\theta<\theta<\tan\theta.$$

answer.short: $A_{\text{sector }OPQ'}=\frac{\theta}{2}$. The inner triangle, sector and outer triangle have strictly increasing areas, so $\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta<\frac{\theta}{2}<\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$. Hence $\sin\theta<\theta<\tan\theta$.
answer.worked:
The sector has radius $1$ and angle $\theta$ radians.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{sector }OPQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\\A_{\text{sector }OPQ'}&=\frac{1}{2}(1)^2\theta\\A_{\text{sector }OPQ'}&=\frac{\theta}{2}.\end{align*}$$

For $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$, triangle $OPQ'$ lies inside the sector, and the sector lies inside triangle $OQQ'$. Each successive region includes a nonzero additional area. Therefore

$$A_{\triangle OPQ'}<A_{\text{sector }OPQ'}<A_{\triangle OQQ'}.$$

Substituting the three areas gives

$$\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta<\frac{\theta}{2}<\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta.$$

Multiplying throughout by $2$ gives

$$\sin\theta<\theta<\tan\theta.$$

answer.short: The graph of $y=\sin x$ lies below $y=x$, which lies below $y=\tan x$, throughout $0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$. Thus $\sin x<x<\tan x$ on this interval.
answer.worked:
Plot the three functions in radian mode over $0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$. The tangent curve rises without bound as $x$ approaches $\frac{\pi}{2}$ from the left.

The sine curve is below the line $y=x$, and the tangent curve is above it throughout the interval. This graphically verifies

content.prompt: Complete the identities using the smallest positive angle in radians, then complete the statement.

answer.worked: Sine repeats after one full revolution, $2\pi$ radians: $\sin(x+2\pi)=\sin x$.
Cosine repeats after one full revolution, $2\pi$ radians: $\cos(x+2\pi)=\cos x$.
Tangent repeats after half a revolution, $\pi$ radians: $\tan(x+\pi)=\tan x$ wherever tangent is defined.
The smallest positive shifts that leave sine, cosine and tangent unchanged are $2\pi$, $2\pi$ and $\pi$ radians respectively. These are their periods.

content.prompt: State the range of the following in the domain $x\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

answer.worked: On $\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $\sin x$ increases from $0$ to $1$. Hence $y\in[0,1]$.
On $\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $\cos x$ decreases from $1$ to $0$. Hence $y\in[0,1]$.
$\tan 0=0$, and $\tan x$ increases without bound as $x$ approaches $\frac{\pi}{2}$ from below. It is undefined at $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Hence $y\in[0,\infty)$.
Where defined, $0<\sin x\leq1$. Taking reciprocals gives $\operatorname{cosec}x\geq1$, with no upper bound as $x$ approaches $0$ from above. Hence $y\in[1,\infty)$.
Where defined, $0<\cos x\leq1$. Taking reciprocals gives $\sec x\geq1$, with no upper bound as $x$ approaches $\frac{\pi}{2}$ from below. Hence $y\in[1,\infty)$.
$\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ decreases from arbitrarily large positive values to $0$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$. It is undefined at $0$. Hence $y\in[0,\infty)$.

content.prompt: State the range of the following in the domain $x\in[-\pi,\pi]$.

answer.worked: The sine graph attains $-1$ at $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $1$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, and takes every value between them. Hence $y\in[-1,1]$.
The cosine graph attains $-1$ at $x=\pm\pi$ and $1$ at $x=0$, and takes every value between them. Hence $y\in[-1,1]$.
Between $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$, the tangent graph takes every real y-value. Hence $y\in(-\infty,\infty)$.
The nonzero sine values lie in $[-1,0)\cup(0,1]$. Their reciprocals give every value at most $-1$ or at least $1$. Hence $y\in(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$.
The nonzero cosine values lie in $[-1,0)\cup(0,1]$. Their reciprocals give every value at most $-1$ or at least $1$. Hence $y\in(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$.
On $0<x<\pi$, $\cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ decreases continuously from arbitrarily large positive values to arbitrarily large negative values. Hence $y\in(-\infty,\infty)$.

answer.worked:
The sine of a complementary angle equals the cosine of the original angle:
$$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\cos x.$$

The cosine of a complementary angle equals the sine of the original angle:
$$\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\sin x.$$

Using the complementary-angle identities, where defined:
$$\begin{align*}\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)&=\frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}\\\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)&=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)&=\cot x.\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Name the quadrant in which $\sin\theta>0$ and $\tan\theta>0$ and hence find the exact value of $\cos\theta$ if $\sin\theta=\frac35$.

answer.worked:
Sine and tangent are both positive in the first quadrant, so cosine is positive.
$$\begin{align*}\cos^2\theta&=1-\sin^2\theta\\\cos^2\theta&=1-\left(\frac35\right)^2=\frac{16}{25}\\\cos\theta&=\frac45.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Name the quadrant in which $\cos\theta<0$ and $\tan\theta>0$ and hence find the exact value of $\sin\theta$ if $\cos\theta=-\frac45$.

answer.worked:
Cosine is negative and tangent is positive in the third quadrant, so sine is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\sin^2\theta&=1-\cos^2\theta\\\sin^2\theta&=1-\left(-\frac45\right)^2=\frac9{25}\\\sin\theta&=-\frac35.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Name the quadrant in which $\sin\theta>0$ and $\tan\theta<0$ and hence find the exact value of $\cot\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ if $\sin\theta=0.7$.

answer.worked:
Sine is positive and tangent is negative in the second quadrant, so cosine is negative. Write $0.7=\frac7{10}$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos^2\theta&=1-\left(\frac7{10}\right)^2\\\cos^2\theta&=\frac{51}{100}\\\cos\theta&=-\frac{\sqrt{51}}{10}\\\cot\theta&=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\\\cot\theta&=\frac{-\frac{\sqrt{51}}{10}}{\frac7{10}}=-\frac{\sqrt{51}}7.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Name the quadrant in which $\sin\theta<0$ and $\cos\theta<0$ and hence find the exact value of $\cot\theta$ if $\sin\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$ and $\cos\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt2}$.

answer.worked:
Sine and cosine are both negative in the third quadrant.
$$\begin{align*}\cot\theta&=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\\\cot\theta&=\frac{-\frac1{\sqrt2}}{-\frac1{\sqrt2}}=1.\end{align*}$$

answer.short: $\frac1{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x=\frac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}=\tan x$, where $\sin x\cos x\ne0$.
answer.worked:
Where $\sin x\cos x\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac1{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac1{\sin x\cos x}-\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\\\frac1{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x\cos x}\\\frac1{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac{\sin^2x}{\sin x\cos x}\\\frac1{\sin x\cos x}-\cot x&=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\tan x.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\frac{\cos^2x-1}{\sin x\cos x}&=\cot x-\frac1{\sin x\cos x}\\\frac{\cos^2x-1}{\sin x\cos x}&=-\tan x.\end{align*}$$
Therefore
$$\begin{align*}-\tan x&=\sqrt3\\\tan x&=-\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Show that the area of the Reuleaux triangle is

answer.short:
$A=\frac{1}{2}(\pi-\sqrt{3})r^2$.

Add three $\frac{\pi}{3}$ sectors and subtract twice the equilateral triangle's area.
answer.worked:
Each circular segment is a sector of angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ minus the equilateral triangle. The Reuleaux triangle consists of that triangle and three such segments.
$$\begin{align*}
A_{\triangle}&=\frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\\
A_{\triangle}&=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2,\\
A_{\text{sector}}&=\frac{1}{2}r^2\times\frac{\pi}{3}\\
A_{\text{sector}}&=\frac{\pi}{6}r^2.
\end{align*}$$
Thus
$$\begin{align*}
A&=A_{\triangle}+3(A_{\text{sector}}-A_{\triangle})\\
A&=3A_{\text{sector}}-2A_{\triangle}\\
A&=3\times\frac{\pi}{6}r^2-2\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}r^2\\
A&=\frac{1}{2}(\pi-\sqrt{3})r^2.
\end{align*}$$

\sin\theta&=\cos\theta\\
\tan\theta&=1\\
\theta&=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4}.
\end{align*}$$
These are the solutions in $[0,2\pi]$.

content.prompt: Use graphing software to sketch $$y=A\sin(nx+\alpha),$$ and create sliders for $A$, $n$ and $\alpha$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Set $\alpha=0$ and $n=1$. Adjust the slider for $A$ and comment on your results.

answer.short: The amplitude is $|A|$. Increasing $|A|$ stretches the graph vertically. Negative $A$ reflects it in the $x$-axis; $A=0$ gives $y=0$.
answer.worked:
With these settings, $y=A\sin x$. Compare the software graphs for $A=1$, $A=2$ and $A=-2$: their ranges are $[-1,1]$, $[-2,2]$ and $[-2,2]$, respectively. The last two graphs are reflections of each other in the $x$-axis.

The amplitude is $|A|$ and, for $A\ne0$, the period remains $2\pi$. At $A=0$, the graph is the $x$-axis.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Set $\alpha=0$ and $A=1$. Adjust the slider for $n$ and comment on your results.

answer.short: For $n\ne0$, the amplitude is $1$ and the period is $\frac{2\pi}{|n|}$. Increasing $|n|$ compresses the graph horizontally. Negative $n$ reflects it in the $y$-axis; $n=0$ gives $y=0$.
answer.worked:
With these settings, $y=\sin(nx)$. On $0\le x\le2\pi$, the software shows one cycle for $n=1$, two cycles for $n=2$ and half a cycle for $n=\frac12$.

Thus increasing $|n|$ shortens the period, while the amplitude remains $1$ for $n\ne0$. One cycle requires a change of $2\pi$ in the argument, so the period is $\frac{2\pi}{|n|}$. Changing the sign of $n$ reflects the graph in the $y$-axis. At $n=0$, every output is $0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Set $A=1$ and $n=1$. Adjust the slider for $\alpha$ and comment on your results.

answer.short: The graph shifts horizontally: left by $\alpha$ when $\alpha>0$, and right by $|\alpha|$ when $\alpha<0$. Its amplitude is $1$ and its period is $2\pi$.
answer.worked:

Changing $\alpha$ translates the graph without changing its amplitude or period. Values of $\alpha$ differing by $2\pi$ give the same graph.

children.prompt: How many metres does the wheel roll after one second?

answer.worked:
In one second, the wheel turns through $\omega$ radians. With no slipping, the distance rolled equals the corresponding arc length.

children.label: b

content.prompt:
[Application to cycling]

A fixed-gear bicycle has the pedals fixed to the front gear. This means that as long as the bicycle is moving, the pedals will always be spinning at a proportional rate. The rear-wheel gear, called the rear sprocket, is much smaller than the front gear, and is connected to it by a chain. It is also directly connected to the rear wheel, which means that the angular speed of the rear wheel will be the same as the angular speed of the rear sprocket.

Consider a bike with a $\frac{58}{14}$ gear-ratio, which means that the front gear has 58 teeth on it whereas the rear sprocket has 14 teeth. Suppose that the radius of the rear sprocket is 3 cm.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Suppose that the number of teeth on the gear is directly proportional to the radius of the gear itself. What is the radius of the front gear?

answer.worked:
Let $r_f$ be the front-gear radius in centimetres.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{r_f}{3}&=\frac{58}{14}\\r_f&=3\times\frac{58}{14}\\r_f&=\frac{87}{7}\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: An Olympic cyclist cycles 50 km after exactly one hour of cycling. Calculate the linear speed of the bicycle, in metres per second. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}v&=\frac{50\,000}{3600}\\v&=\frac{125}{9}\text{ m/s}\\v&\approx13.89\text{ m/s}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: The chain transfers the tangential speed of the rear sprocket rim to the front gear. Let the rear-wheel radius be $R$ metres and assume the bicycle rolls without slipping. Find the angular speed of the front gear in terms of $R$.

answer.short: A numerical answer cannot be determined: the rear-wheel radius is missing. For rear-wheel radius $R$ metres, $\omega_f=\frac{875}{261R}\text{ rad/s}$.
answer.worked:
The chain transfers the tangential speed of the sprocket rim. This is different from the bicycle's forward speed. Let the rear-wheel radius be $R$ metres, and assume rolling without slipping.
$$\begin{align*}\omega_r&=\frac{v}{R}\\\omega_r&=\frac{125}{9R}\text{ rad/s}\\\omega_f&=\frac{14}{58}\omega_r\\\omega_f&=\frac{14}{58}\times\frac{125}{9R}\\\omega_f&=\frac{875}{261R}\text{ rad/s}.\end{align*}$$
A numerical value requires the rear-wheel radius or circumference.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence, determine how many revolutions per minute the Olympian had to output, on average, for the whole hour.

answer.short: A numerical cadence cannot be determined without the rear-wheel radius. For radius $R$ metres, the cadence is $\frac{8750}{87\pi R}\text{ rpm}$.
answer.worked:
The pedals and front gear rotate together. One revolution is $2\pi$ radians.
$$\begin{align*}n&=\frac{60\omega_f}{2\pi}\\n&=\frac{60}{2\pi}\times\frac{875}{261R}\\n&=\frac{8750}{87\pi R}\text{ rpm}.\end{align*}$$
The missing rear-wheel measurement prevents a numerical result.

content.prompt: Research the linear speeds of a typical Olympic cyclist when doing the ‘hour record’. Using the techniques from Question 5, find how many revolutions per minute they were pedalling at (called the cadence), on average. Now research the typical speed of an average cyclist (or even yourself!) and compare.

answer.short: Answers vary. For speed $v$ km/h, wheel circumference $C$ metres and gear ratio $G$ (front teeth divided by rear teeth), cadence is $\frac{50v}{3CG}\text{ rpm}$. Speed alone does not determine cadence.
answer.worked:
For a fixed-gear bicycle rolling without slipping, let $v$ be speed in km/h, $C$ the wheel circumference in metres and $G$ the front-to-rear tooth ratio. One pedal revolution produces $G$ wheel revolutions, covering $CG$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}\text{distance per minute}&=\frac{1000v}{60}\text{ m}\\\text{cadence}&=\frac{1000v}{60CG}\\\text{cadence}&=\frac{50v}{3CG}\text{ rpm}.\end{align*}$$
Use each cyclist's speed, wheel circumference and gear ratio to calculate their cadence. Compare the two speeds and cadences. If both bicycles have the same circumference and gearing, their cadence ratio equals their speed ratio. Otherwise, compare the calculated cadences separately. There is no single numerical answer without the researched data.

entries.description: How many metres does the wheel roll after one second?
Hence, what is the linear speed s of the wheel?

[Application to cycling]
A fixed-gear bicycle has the pedals fixed to the front gear. This means that as long as the bicycle is moving, the pedals will always be spinning at a proportional rate. The rear-wheel gear, called the rear sprocket, is much smaller than the front gear, and is connected to it by a chain. It is also directly connected to the rear wheel, which means that the angular speed of the rear wheel will be the same as the angular speed of the rear sprocket.

Consider a bike with a 58/14 gear-ratio, which means that the front gear has 58 teeth on it whereas the rear sprocket has 14 teeth. Suppose that the radius of the rear sprocket is 3 cm.
